channel_name: No Priors · Elad Gil & Sarah Guo
video_title: Powering AI-Driven Drug Discovery with President of Isomorphic Labs Max Jaderberg
gist: Isomorphic Labs president Max Jaderberg argues pharma's flat drug output and ~$1.5B/15-year cost stem from empirical trial-and-error, and that Isomorphic's in-house, disease-agnostic AI drug design engine (built on AlphaFold-style models and proprietary data) can push predictions to experimental accuracy, cut clinical failure from unforeseen toxicity, and enable safer combination therapies. Isomorphic owns rather than licenses its models, runs internal oncology and immunology programs plus pharma partnerships, and is building a clinical team ahead of first trials.

insights.claim: New drug approvals per year have stayed roughly flat even as scientific papers grew 10-20x, new modalities multiplied, cost per drug rose from a few hundred million to about $1.5B and timelines stretched from 8-9 to ~15 years.
insights.speaker: host (Elad Gil)
insights.so_what: Eroom's-law style productivity decline is the core inefficiency AI drug discovery platforms claim to arbitrage; watch whether AI-native pipelines bend approval-per-dollar curves.

insights.claim: Max Jaderberg attributes pharma's stagnation to a still largely empirical make-and-test process that has harvested the low-hanging fruit, leaving higher-complexity medicines out of reach of trial-and-error screening.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Value accrues to platforms that can search combinatorially large molecular design spaces computationally rather than by screening.
insights.quote: We're finding the low hanging fruit, but then it's getting harder and harder to sort of ratchet up the complexity

insights.claim: Traditional pharma treats each drug program as a bespoke frontier science project with little transferable learning, so R&D lacks economies of scale; an AI platform could produce compounding improvements the more medicines it pursues.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: The investable thesis for AI-native drug developers is compounding platform returns across programs, unlike single-asset biotechs.

insights.claim: Apart from Moderna, which the host calls almost an accident of COVID, no new biopharma company has reached $50B+ value since the 1980s era of Regeneron, Vertex and Amgen, suggesting industry aging and bureaucracy slow innovation much as in autos before Tesla.
insights.speaker: host (Elad Gil)
insights.so_what: Implies an opening for a new large-cap biopharma built on a structurally different R&D engine.

insights.claim: Clinical failure, driven by unforeseen toxicity, off-target effects or harmful on-target biology discovered only in patients, is the main driver of drug development costs.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Any technology that predicts human toxicity pre-clinically attacks the largest cost bucket; clinical success rates are the KPI to watch.
insights.quote: where things really fail is in the clinic

insights.claim: The host estimates the discovery and preclinical phase takes 2-3 years and roughly $50M, while ~$1.45B and ~12 years of the ~$1.5B, 15-year process is spent in clinical trials.
insights.speaker: host (Elad Gil)
insights.so_what: AI that only speeds discovery addresses a small share of cost; the payoff requires raising clinical probability of success.

insights.claim: Isomorphic Labs' north star is moving drug discovery and design onto a computer, because synthesizing real atoms and running assays is the fundamental time and cost bottleneck.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Positions Isomorphic as a computation-first rather than lab-automation-first player in AI drug discovery.
insights.quote: fundamentally the the big time bottleneck the big cost bottleneck is synthesizing real atoms

insights.claim: Isomorphic tracks an 'experimental accuracy' line on all internal model leaderboards; once a predictive model reaches it, the corresponding real-world experiment can be skipped, raising probability of success when molecules are finally made.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: A useful benchmark lens for evaluating AI-bio claims: does the model match experimental accuracy for a given step?
insights.quote: we have you know a dotted line on all of our leaderboards that is experimental accuracy

insights.claim: AlphaFold illustrates the approach: structure prediction that used to take months or years of X-ray crystallography can be done by a simulation model.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Structural biology services and crystallography workflows face substitution from predictive models.

insights.claim: AlphaFold's results around 2018-2019 were the proof of concept that deep learning could generalize meaningfully in biology, which led DeepMind veterans including Demis to found Isomorphic Labs in about 2021.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Isomorphic is Alphabet's dedicated vehicle to commercialize DeepMind's biology breakthroughs.

insights.claim: Isomorphic does not sell or license its model or tokens; it uses the drug design engine internally to make medicines through wholly owned programs and through partnerships with pharma and biotech companies.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Business model is asset ownership plus partnership economics, not SaaS; value capture depends on clinical outcomes.
insights.quote: we actually, you know, don't sell the model. We we don't license out the model. We don't sell tokens in that way.

insights.claim: Pharma partners bring Isomorphic their hardest problems, sometimes worked on for 10-20 years without progress, which Isomorphic claims its engine can advance substantially.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Partnership milestones on previously intractable targets are a signal of platform validity.

insights.claim: Isomorphic's internal pipeline focuses on oncology and immunology/inflammation, while its models are disease-, target-class- and modality-agnostic.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Watch oncology and I&I for Isomorphic's first clinical assets.

insights.claim: Isomorphic targets 'root node' mechanisms that drive many downstream indications, citing Revolution Medicines' RAS inhibitor that won a standing ovation for improving outcomes in late-stage pancreatic cancer.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Validates pan-indication driver targets like RAS as high-value; Revolution Medicines is a reference success for hard-target oncology.

insights.claim: Isomorphic has not given a date for its first clinical trial but says its medicines are progressing well and it has been building a clinical development team.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Clinical entry is the next major de-risking catalyst for Isomorphic and for Alphabet's bio optionality.
insights.quote: We've been building up our clinical development team.

insights.claim: Isomorphic is hiring top AI researchers for core simulation models like 'AlphaFold++' and for adapting frontier and open-source reasoning models to drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Signals a roadmap combining physical-simulation models with LLM-style reasoning agents for biology.

insights.claim: Existing public and pharma data repositories are biased byproducts of passive data collection, so Isomorphic generates its own proprietary data for generalization and reports strong data scaling laws as a result.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Proprietary, purpose-generated datasets, not legacy pharma archives, may be the real moat in AI drug discovery.
insights.quote: we've seen some really really amazing uh data scaling laws as a result

insights.claim: Isomorphic builds all AI models in-house but works with CROs and other companies to generate the data powering its models.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: AI-native drug developers are a demand source for CROs and specialized experimental platforms.

insights.claim: Automated and robotic labs, like the wet lab Anthropic reportedly is building, help shorten iteration, but physics caps them since reactions and cell cultures take fixed time, so the bigger lever is reducing real-world experimentation via in-silico prediction.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Lab-automation plays face diminishing returns relative to predictive-model plays; real-world experiments shift from learning to validation.
insights.quote: fundamentally I want to get out of the real world

insights.claim: Rat toxicity studies, the regulatory gold standard, are only about 30% predictive of human clinical toxicity.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Large opening for human-relevant tox prediction (AI plus in-vitro) to displace or augment animal testing.
insights.quote: it's about 30% predictive of of of human clinical tox

insights.claim: Combining in-vitro endpoints, AI predictive models and new organoid and organ-on-a-chip technologies could directly model human clinical toxicity, although clinical-trial data is limited.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Organoid and organ-on-chip platforms are complementary beneficiaries of AI-driven safety prediction.

insights.claim: Drug cocktails are underused in cancer because individual molecules carry toxicity and liver effects that cause harmful drug-drug interactions; more precisely engineered molecules could enable complex combinations hitting a whole vector of targets.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Cleaner AI-designed molecules could unlock a combination-therapy market, mirroring HIV cocktails.

insights.claim: Tumors contain a spectrum of mutations and evolve around single drugs, so multi-drug cocktails like those used for HIV may be required to cure cancer.
insights.speaker: host (Elad Gil)
insights.so_what: Supports the value of combinable, low-toxicity molecules and portfolios of complementary assets.

insights.claim: Max Jaderberg argues safety should stay central but regulatory risk tolerance should vary with patient need, e.g. late-stage cancer versus chronic low-level inflammation, as COVID showed.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Indication choice affects regulatory speed; high-unmet-need oncology offers more permissive risk-benefit paths.

insights.claim: Isomorphic expects AI-designed molecules to show statistically different success rates and safety profiles, which it hopes will change how regulators approach getting drugs to patients.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: If proven, AI-designed drugs could earn faster regulatory pathways, compounding the time advantage.

insights.claim: The host cites Janssen Pharmaceuticals founder Paul Janssen's view that an overemphasis on safety is the main constraint on drug development, pointing to the rapid WWII commercialization of penicillin once regulatory obstacles were removed.
insights.speaker: host (Elad Gil)
insights.so_what: Regulatory loosening is a latent upside catalyst for drug-development throughput.

insights.claim: Max Jaderberg would be disappointed if within five years predictive understanding of disease biology and the ability to design more precise, less toxic molecules have not step-changed massively.
insights.speaker: Max Jaderberg
insights.so_what: Sets a ~5-year window to judge whether AI drug discovery is delivering versus hype.
insights.quote: I'd be really disappointed if we fast forward, you know, even five years time

insights.claim: The host notes that eliminating cancer and heart disease would add only roughly five to seven years to average lifespan, while gene knockouts in model organisms extend life 20-30% in flies and mice and threefold in C. elegans, extending health span along with lifespan.
insights.speaker: host (Elad Gil)
insights.so_what: Targeting aging itself may offer larger health outcomes than single-disease programs, a longer-dated investment theme.
